beats.say: Most club games aren't lost in the opening. They're lost in the middlegame, when nobody knows what to do next.
So here's the deal. Learn one setup in ten minutes, play it nearly every game, and spend the time you save on the part that actually decides games.
Think of it as a morning routine. Same seven moves, same order. You can do it half asleep and still leave the house with your shoes on.
We'll build the setup, deal with the five ways Black tries to spoil it, learn the one punch, then watch it land in two games.
Seven moves. Watch the list tick itself off.
Pawn to d4. Your queen already guards it.
Bishop out, right now. This is the one move order you must not get wrong.
Now e3. Play it one move sooner and that bishop spends the whole game locked in a cupboard.
Knight to f3. It looks at e5. Remember that square.
The other knight goes to d2, behind the first one, leaving the c-pawn free to move.
c3 finishes the pyramid. Black can hit that d-pawn as often as they like.
Bishop to d3, staring straight at the black king's front door. That's it. The setup is done.
Now look at what your pieces agree on: e5. Pawn, bishop, knight. That one square is the whole plan.
Your opponent didn't read the script. Here are the five things they'll try, and you only need one answer to each.

beats.reset: d4 d5 Bf4 Nf6 e3 e6 Nf3 c5 c3 Nc6 Nbd2 Be7 Bd3
beats.say: One. Black kicks your bishop with the c-pawn.
Drop back one square. Same diagonal, same target. That bishop only cares about h7.

beats.reset: d4 d5 Bf4 Nf6 e3 e6 Nf3
beats.say: Two. Black offers to trade your best bishop.
Don't take. The queen recaptures on d6, and the piece fighting for e5 has gone.
Slide back to g3 and stay on the diagonal. Stockfish rates this and the trade about equal, so you're keeping your plan, not winning anything.
If they take, take back with the h-pawn. Your rook now has the h-file, right where Black wants to castle, for free.

beats.reset: d4 d5 Bf4 Bf5 e3 e6 Nf3 Nf6
beats.say: Three. Black copies you with Bf5, and that bishop owns the diagonal you wanted.
Challenge it with your own bishop. Don't capture. Stand there and let them decide.
If they take, your queen lands on a good square. The engine calls it level, and the threat to your setup has gone.

beats.reset: d4 d5 Bf4 Nf6 e3 e6 Nf3
beats.say: Four. A bishop check, usually played to knock you off your routine.
You wanted c3 anyway. Now it arrives with an attack on the bishop.
Black has spent two moves getting the bishop to e7. You carry on with the list.

beats.reset: d4 d5 Bf4 Nf6 e3 c5 c3
beats.say: Five. Queen to b6, hitting b2. Your bishop left home early, so that pawn has lost its guard.
Put your own queen in the way. No pawn drops, and the queens stare at each other.
If they trade, your a-pawn takes back and your rook gets the a-file. The pawns look ugly, but the engine still prefers White.

chapters.title: The punch
chapters.from: d4 d5 Bf4 Nf6 e3 e6 Nf3 Be7 Nbd2 O-O c3 c5 Bd3 Nc6

beats.say: Back to the finished setup. Your pieces have been staring at e5 for a reason.
The knight jumps in, guarded by the pawn and the bishop.
Taking feels natural, but it's a small mistake. The engine goes from about plus 0.2 to about plus 0.8.
Take back with the pawn, and now that pawn is hitting the knight on f6.
It has to move. And the quiet part: your f3 knight left, so the road from d1 to h5 is open.
Queen to h5. Queen and bishop both hit h7, and that threatens mate next move.
A warning. This isn't a forced win. With g6, Black holds, and the engine says White is about half a pawn better. But one slip, like h6, and it's above plus three.

beats.reset: d4 d5 Bf4 Nf6 e3 e6 Nf3 Be7 Nbd2 O-O c3 c5 Bd3 Nc6 Ne5
beats.say: And they don't have to take. Knight to d7 is the best reply. You haven't lost anything: keep developing, and castle.

beats.card: Game one: it goes to plan
beats.say: This game is made up by us and checked by Stockfish. Black's moves are all natural ones.

beats.play: d4 d5 Bf4 Nf6 e3 e6 Nf3
beats.say: The routine. Nothing to think about yet.
A check. You've seen this one.
c3, and the bishop has to go.
Setup done. Black's fine. And now you already know your next move.
The knight jumps in.
They take. You take back, hitting the knight.
It runs, and here comes the queen.
Black blocks with g6, and it's safe for now. But look at the holes around that king: f6 and h6.
So move in. Queen to h6, sitting on the dark squares like it pays rent.
Here Black's best is f6, hitting your pawn, and then the game is close to level. So far you've made no threat they can't meet.
But most people want their own attack, so c5. That's the mistake. It takes the engine from about plus 0.4 to above plus three.
Bring the last piece. The knight's going to g5, and from there it hits h7 as well.
Black keeps pushing on the other side of the board.
Knight to g5. Now it's mate on h7 unless Black gives something up.
Black takes the knight, and that gets rid of the bishop guarding the dark squares.
Your bishop takes back, and it hits the queen on the way.
The queen steps aside, though f6 was the last real chance. What's missing? A queen on g7 would be mate, if only something guarded that square.
So guard it. Bishop to f6. Black can't take it and escape.
The knight takes.
And your e5 pawn takes back. A pawn on f6 guards g7 just as well as the bishop did.
Nothing can stop it. Black's queen can't reach g7, and the king has no way out.
Checkmate. And count Black's mistakes: only one or two, and neither looked like much at the time.
Also ours, also engine-checked. This time Black opens with e6. Doesn't matter. Play the routine.
Bishop out. And Black's d5 brings us straight back to known ground.
Reply number two from the list: the bishop trade.
Back to g3. They take. The h-pawn takes back, and your rook has the h-file.

beats.play: Nf6 Nf3 c5 c3 Nc6 Nbd2 Qe7
beats.say: A few quiet moves. Same setup as always, with one bishop fewer.
Setup done, and Black castles. Look at h7: your bishop and your rook both point at it.
So you play the same knight jump as always.
In game one, taking cost Black a little. Here it loses on the spot.
Think it through. Bishop and rook want h7. The king can't take a guarded piece, so only the knight on f6 defends it. What if that knight had to leave?
It has to. The same pawn recapture from the punch, and now the defender is under attack.
The knight runs, and h7 has lost its defender.
Bishop takes with check.
The king steps into the corner, right in line with your rook. The only thing between them is your own bishop.
So move the bishop. Discovered check from the rook.
The longest defence is to throw the queen in the way.
Thank you. The rook takes it, and the king goes back.
One flourish left. Give up the rook, just to drag the king into the corner.
Black has to take. And your queen's road to h5 is open again.
Check, the king goes back, and that bishop has been waiting on h7 the whole time.
Checkmate, all from one knight jump, because Black took on e5 without looking at h7.

chapters.title: Your game plan
chapters.from: d4 d5 Bf4 Nf6 e3 e6 Nf3 Be7 Nbd2 O-O c3 c5 Bd3 Nc6

beats.card: So how do you win with this?
beats.say: The opening is the easy part. Here's the whole plan in three lines.
One. Play the seven moves, and meet the five annoying replies with the answers you just saw.
Two. When the setup is done, jump to e5.
Three. If they take, take back with the pawn, then bring the queen to h5. With your rook on the h-file, look at taking on h7 as well.
That's a good way to win quick games. It isn't a middlegame plan. A careful opponent answers with f6 or knight to d7, the attack fizzles, and then you have to think.
So do two things next. Play the setup from memory until your hands know it, then read the London plan for what to do when the punch doesn't land.
